overview:
In Jain philosophy, **jīva tattva** refers to the fundamental reality of living beings—sentient, conscious substances that possess inherent qualities such as knowledge, perception, bliss, energy, and the capacity for liberation. As one of the core *tattvas* (ontological categories), jīva is central to Jain metaphysics, ethics, and soteriology. Jain thinkers across traditions—Digambara, Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth—agree that jīva is beginningless, eternal, and distinct from *ajīva* (non-living substances). 

Jīvas are infinite in number and vary in embodiment, ranging from liberated souls (*siddhas*) to embodied beings entangled in karmic matter. The defining characteristic of jīva is **upayoga**, the activity of consciousness, expressed as knowledge (*jñāna*) and perception (*darśana*). When obscured by karma, these qualities appear limited; when karma is destroyed, the soul manifests its pure, infinite nature. 

Jain texts classify jīvas by the number of sense faculties (from one-sensed beings like plants to five-sensed beings like humans), by mobility (immobile vs. mobile), and by spiritual development (from the lowest states to the highest *guṇasthānas*). This taxonomy supports Jain ethics: recognizing the presence of jīva in all forms of life grounds the commitment to nonviolence (*ahiṃsā*). 

In liberation, the jīva becomes a *siddha*, residing at the apex of the universe (*siddha-śilā*), free from karma, omniscient, and possessing infinite energy and bliss. Thus, jīva tattva is not merely a metaphysical category but the foundation of Jain spiritual practice, guiding the aspirant from bondage to freedom.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation: The living being is (defined as) that which possesses consciousness.
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha Sūtra 2.8 provides the canonical definition of jīva as the substance characterized by consciousness (*caitanya*). Both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions accept this text, though commentarial interpretations differ.

primary_sources.title: Dravyasaṃgraha
primary_sources.author: Nemicandra Siddhānta Cakravartin
primary_sources.translation: The characteristic of the soul is upayoga, the activity of consciousness.
primary_sources.notes: A Digambara primer on Jain ontology. This verse emphasizes *upayoga* as the essential mark of jīva, elaborated in later commentaries.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Attributed to Mahāvīra’s disciples
primary_sources.translation: All living beings, all creatures (are to be regarded with care).
primary_sources.notes: A foundational Śvetāmbara text emphasizing the universality of life and the ethical implications of recognizing jīva in all forms.

misconceptions.myth: Jīva is identical to the physical body.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts consistently teach that jīva is a distinct, eternal substance that merely occupies a body due to karmic bondage.
Jain ontology affirms jīva in plants, microorganisms, animals, and celestial and infernal beings, each with varying sensory capacities.

misconceptions.myth: Liberated souls retain subtle karmic traces or individuality shaped by past lives.
misconceptions.reality: A siddha is completely free from all karmic matter; individuality remains only as the unique identity of the soul, not as personality or memory.
